title: RF exposure
idea: RF is non-ionizing: it heats, it doesn't damage DNA. How much you get depends on frequency, power, distance and the antenna pattern, averaged over how much of the time you transmit. The station licensee answers for it.

items: Non-ionizing radiation. Not enough energy to cause chemical changes in cells or damage DNA
50 MHz. The body absorbs more RF at some frequencies than others
Frequency and power, distance, and the antenna's radiation pattern
The percentage of time you're transmitting. It affects the average exposure
Calculation (OET Bulletin 65 or computer modeling) or measurement with calibrated equipment
Re-evaluate whenever the transmitter or antenna system changes

config.heading: RF safety, case by case
config.lead: Pick a case. Some let you change a setting.

situations.label: Is RF like radioactivity?
situations.title: No: non-ionizing
situations.text: Radio signals are non-ionizing radiation. They don't have enough energy to cause chemical changes in cells and damage DNA.

situations.label: Which band has the strictest limit?
situations.title: Exposure limits

rules.title: 50 MHz: the lowest limit of these
rules.text: Of these bands, 50 MHz has the lowest maximum permissible exposure. Limits vary with frequency because the body absorbs more RF at some frequencies than at others.

rules.title: A higher limit than 50 MHz
rules.text: This band's limit is higher than 50 MHz's. Limits vary because the body absorbs more RF energy at some frequencies than at others.

situations.label: Someone stands near my antenna
situations.title: Four things set their exposure
situations.text: The frequency and power level of the RF field, the distance from the antenna, and the antenna's radiation pattern. All of them count.

situations.label: I transmit less of the time
situations.title: Duty cycle

rules.title: Transmitting all the time
rules.text: Duty cycle is the percentage of time a transmitter is transmitting. It matters because it affects the average exposure.

rules.title: Allowed power density doubles
rules.text: Going from 100% to 50% duty cycle increases the allowable power density by a factor of 2, because the average exposure halves.

situations.label: Does my station comply?
situations.title: Calculate or measure
situations.text: Calculation based on FCC OET Bulletin 65, calculation based on computer modeling, or measurement with calibrated equipment: any of them is acceptable. Re-evaluate whenever an item in the transmitter or antenna system changes.

situations.label: Lower the exposure near my station
situations.title: Relocate antennas
situations.text: Moving the antennas reduces exposure. Moving the transmitter doesn't help, and a higher duty cycle makes it worse.

situations.label: Touch the antenna while transmitting
situations.title: RF burn to skin
situations.text: Touching an antenna during a transmission can cause an RF burn to the skin. It isn't ionizing radiation.

situations.label: Who answers for it?
situations.title: The station licensee
situations.text: The station licensee is responsible for making sure no person is exposed to RF energy above the FCC limits.

compare.how: Not enough energy to change cells or damage DNA.
Gamma and alpha radiation. Not what radio signals are.

traps.why: Higher frequency doesn't mean a stricter limit. Of these, 50 MHz has the lowest.
Halving the duty cycle doubles the allowable power density. It doesn't cut it.

traps.wrong: Distance from the antenna to a person
traps.why: Distance matters, but so do frequency, power and the radiation pattern. It's all of them.

traps.wrong: Lower frequency RF fields have more energy than higher frequency fields
traps.why: It's not about energy per frequency. The body absorbs more RF at some frequencies than others.

traps.wrong: By measurement of field strength using calibrated equipment
traps.why: Measurement works, but so do both kinds of calculation. Any of them is acceptable.
The hazard is an RF burn to the skin.
Moving the transmitter doesn't help. Moving the antennas does.

traps.wrong: By making sure your antennas have low SWR
traps.why: Low SWR isn't RF safety. Re-evaluate whenever the transmitter or antenna system changes.

traps.wrong: It affects the peak exposure to radiation
traps.why: Duty cycle affects the average exposure, not the peak.

traps.wrong: The percentage of time that a transmitter is not transmitting
traps.why: Duty cycle is the time spent transmitting, not the time off.
RF isn't perfectly safe. It just can't change cells or damage DNA the way ionizing radiation can.
Not the FCC. The station licensee is responsible.
